papers.title: A Modular Cryogenic Link for Microwave Quantum Communication Over Distances of Tens of Meters
papers.abstract: Quantum technologies promise a radically new way to solve classically intractable computing problems. Superconducting circuits as a platform are at the forefront of this field. The cryogenic operation temperatures of superconducting circuits however impose challenges for the further scaling to many connected quantum information processing units into a local area or global network. In this work, we present a hardware solution for connecting quantum devices operating at microwave frequencies into local area networks, which enable the exchange of quantum information between spatially separated parties. Specifically, we demonstrate a modular system spanning distances of 5, 10 and 30 meters operated at cryogenic temperatures and connecting two superconducting circuit systems, located in individual dilution refrigerators, through a quantum communication channel. We develop a thermal model to evaluate the heat transfer processes in the setup, optimize the design and select appropriate materials for its construction. The assembled 30-meter-long system achieves operating temperatures of below 50 mK after a cooldown time of about six and a half days. This link enables the execution of distributed quantum computing and communication algorithms. It also adds the resource of non-locality, certified by a loophole-free Bell test, to the field of quantum science and technology with superconducting circuits.

similar_to.title: A Modular Cryogenic Link for Microwave Quantum Communication Over Distances of Tens of Meters
Wireless millikelvin interconnects for superconducting quantum hardware

summary.summary: A modular cryogenic link comprising superconducting radiation shields, copper braids, and a WR90 waveguide connects two dilution refrigerators over 30 meters while maintaining millikelvin temperatures and enabling quantum communication between spatially separated superconducting qubits. The system achieves base temperatures below 50 mK along its entire length with a 6.5-day cooldown time, and detailed thermal modeling predicts extensions to 120 m using additional cooling units spaced at 15 m intervals.
summary.motivation: Scaling superconducting quantum processors into distributed networks requires connecting cryogenic systems over meter-scale distances while preserving quantum coherence; microwave quantum communication channels operating in cryogenic environments offer high-fidelity, broadband entanglement distribution without the conversion losses and added noise that plague microwave-to-optical transduction approaches.
summary.method: A hierarchical modular architecture (link modules, adapter modules, braid modules, and a central cooling unit) contains octagonal copper radiation shields at five temperature stages, minimizes radiative and conductive heat loads through multi-layer insulation ($\phi_\mathrm{rad} \approx 1$ W/m$^2$ on 50K shield), Bluestone support posts, and high-purity OFE copper with RRR $\approx 210$. Thermal modeling based on Stefan-Boltzmann radiation, Fourier heat conduction, and measured contact resistances ($R_\mathrm{contact} \propto T^{-2}$ below 10 K) guided design optimization.
summary.result: The 30 m system reaches steady-state temperatures of 10–15 mK at the nodes and below 50 mK throughout the link, with 4K and 50K stages staying below 6 K and 80 K respectively; waveguide attenuation is $\alpha < 1$ dB/km (0.03 dB total loss over 30 m), and the system maintains stable operation for approximately 6 months before O-ring seals degrade; thermal extrapolations indicate 120 m links are feasible with cooling units every 15 m.

papers.title: Fast, High-Fidelity Erasure Detection of Dual-Rail Qubits with Symmetrically Coupled Readout
papers.abstract: Erasure qubits are a promising platform for implementing hardware-efficient quantum error correction. Realizing the error-correction advantages of this encoding requires frequent mid-circuit erasure checks that are fast, high-fidelity, and scalable. Here, we realize erasure detection with a hardware-efficient circuit consisting of a single readout resonator dispersively and symmetrically coupled to both transmons of a dual-rail qubit. We use this circuit to demonstrate single-shot erasure detection in 384 ns with minimal impact on the dual-rail logical manifold, achieving a residual error per check of $6.0(2) \times 10^{-4}$, with only $8(3) \times 10^{-5}$ induced dephasing per check, and an erasure error per check of $2.54(1)\times 10^{-2}$. The high degree of matched dispersive readout coupling ($χ$-matching) within the dual-rail qubit code space also allows us to realize a new modality: time-continuous erasure detection performed in parallel with single-qubit gates. Here we achieve a median $7.2 \times 10^{-5}$ error per gate with $< 1 \times 10^{-5}$ error induced by erasure detection. This demonstrates a reduction in erasure detection overhead as well as a crucial ingredient for soft information quantum error correction. Together, these results establish symmetrically coupled dispersive readout as a fast, hardware-efficient, and scalable component for erasure-based quantum error correction using transmon dual-rail qubits.

similar_to.title: Fast, High-Fidelity Erasure Detection of Dual-Rail Qubits with Symmetrically Coupled Readout
Demonstrating a long-coherence dual-rail erasure qubit using tunable transmons

summary.summary: This paper demonstrates high-fidelity mid-circuit erasure detection in transmon dual-rail qubits using a symmetrically coupled readout resonator (SRO), achieving 384 ns erasure checks with $6.0(2) \times 10^{-4}$ residual error per check and enabling continuous parallel erasure detection during gates at $7.2 \times 10^{-5}$ error per X90 gate. The symmetric coupling achieves $\chi$-matching with $|\chi_{\mathrm{DR}}/\chi| < 1 \times 10^{-2}$ over 600 MHz, suppressing measurement-induced dephasing while maintaining strong erasure-state discrimination.
summary.motivation: Erasure qubits offer higher error thresholds and favorable scaling for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but realizing their advantages requires frequent, fast, high-fidelity mid-circuit erasure checks that minimally disturb the logical subspace—a challenge for previous superconducting implementations with significant overhead or long detection times.
summary.method: A single readout resonator is dispersively and symmetrically coupled to both transmons in a dual-rail pair, with engineered symmetric couplings ($g_{\mathrm{RT1}} = g_{\mathrm{RT2}}$) achieving a zero-crossing of $\chi_{\mathrm{DR}}$ near 4.5 GHz where the logical states experience matched dispersive shifts. Single-shot readout uses 384 ns probes optimized for signal-to-noise ratio while minimizing measurement-induced state transitions; continuous parallel detection exploits $\chi$-matching to monitor erasure events during gate execution.
summary.result: Single-shot erasure detection achieves $2.54(1) \times 10^{-2}$ erasure error and $6.0(2) \times 10^{-4}$ residual error per 384 ns check with $8(3) \times 10^{-5}$ induced dephasing; continuous parallel erasure detection during single-qubit gates yields $7.2 \times 10^{-5}$ X90 error with $< 1 \times 10^{-5}$ detection overhead, demonstrating erasure detection overhead reduction and temporal resolution beneficial for soft-information quantum error correction.

papers.title: Digital Predistortion for Flux Control of Tunable Superconducting Qubits
papers.abstract: Flux-tunable superconducting qubits rely on fast flux control pulses to implement two-qubit entangling quantum gates, a key building block for quantum algorithms. However, distortion effects introduced by non-ideal control electronics, parasitic components, and the cryogenic quantum chip response can all degrade the gate fidelity. We present a digital predistortion (DPD) framework for characterizing and then compensating for these distortions using a combination of infinite impulse response (IIR) and finite impulse response (FIR) filters. Experiments on a flux-tunable quantum processing unit (QPU) demonstrate a successful correction of step-response distortions on the flux-control line, with a compensated control signal showing only sub-percent deviations from the ideal target linear behavior. The demonstrated method enables automated rapid calibration of flux control channels for superconducting QPUs.

similar_to.title: Suppressing Counter-Rotating Errors for Fast Single-Qubit Gates with Fluxonium
The Flux Qubit Revisited to Enhance Coherence and Reproducibility

summary.summary: This paper presents a digital predistortion (DPD) framework using cascaded IIR and FIR filters to compensate for distortion in flux-control signals of superconducting qubits, achieving sub-percent deviations from ideal behavior. Experiments on a 20-qubit IQM Garnet QPU demonstrate correction of combined classical (AWG, cryogenic line, bias-tee) and quantum chip voltage-to-flux transfer function distortions using Cryoscope characterization.
summary.motivation: Flux-tunable qubits require fast, accurate control pulses for two-qubit CZ gates, but non-ideal electronics, parasitic components, and cryogenic response degrade gate fidelity; compensating distortions avoids costly settling delays.
summary.method: Distortion sources (AWG modeled as second-order underdamped system with time constants 1–100 ns; cryo line exponential overshoot 1 ns–10 µs; bias-tee 10 µs–10 ms) are characterized via 2D flux spectroscopy and Cryoscope Ramsey measurements to extract the voltage-to-flux transfer function, then inverted to calculate IIR ($M_a=1$, $M_b=2$) and FIR filter coefficients via linear least-squares optimization.
summary.result: IIR correction alone achieves 0.65% deviation from ideal linear response; cascaded FIR filtering reduces this to 0.17% deviation with $\log(\mathrm{NMSE}) < -30$ dB, using measured $T_1 = 21.5$ µs and $T_2^* = 4.9$ µs on qubit Q1.

papers.title: A digitally controlled silicon quantum processing unit
authors: Members of the HRL Quantum Team
papers.abstract: Commercially-relevant quantum computers will require large numbers of high-performing qubits that can be manufactured, integrated, and controlled at scale. Silicon exchange-only (EO) qubits are a strong candidate modality due to their control-signal simplicity and compatibility with advanced semiconductor manufacturing, but questions remain around the achievability of sufficiently low noise and a scalable control and wiring solution. Here we introduce a quantum processing unit composed of a custom-designed cryogenic CMOS controller, a novel high-density superconducting ribbon cable, and a low-noise EO qubit device. The quantum chip features a three-rail array of 54 exchange-coupled quantum dots, configurable to host up to 18 EO qubits. We integrate and use these components to demonstrate qubit performance for both single-qubit and entangling operations that advances the EO state of the art by an order of magnitude. We further validate this system by implementing a distance-5 repetition code and a quantum error detecting code then make detailed comparisons with simulations. Our approach facilitates a utility-scale quantum computer with manageable operational and capital requirements.

similar_to.title: A digitally controlled silicon quantum processing unit
Quantum Computer Controlled by Superconducting Digital Electronics at Millikelvin Temperature

summary.summary: This work demonstrates a fully integrated silicon exchange-only qubit processing unit combining a custom cryogenic CMOS controller at 4 K, a superconducting Nb/polyimide ribbon cable, and a 54-dot quantum chip, achieving single-qubit gate errors of $2 	imes 10^{-4}$ and CNOT errors of $3 	imes 10^{-3}$—an order of magnitude improvement over prior EO qubits. The system validates quantum error correction capability through distance-5 repetition codes and a [[4,2,2]] quantum error detecting code with logical fidelities of $F_L = 0.95$ post-selected.
summary.motivation: Silicon spin qubits have advanced rapidly but system-level control and integration lag behind qubit performance; a scalable architecture is needed that avoids the "wiring bottleneck" of room-temperature control while managing cryogenic heat loads.
summary.method: A cryo-CMOS controller (130 nm, 70 million transistors, ≤3.5 W) at 4 K generates 150 time-varying voltage signals via 366 DACs and 78 pulse generators with $\approx$1 ps timing resolution, routed through a high-density superconducting ribbon cable (296 lines on polyimide, <10 μW thermal load, <−80 dB crosstalk at 10 GHz) to mK qubits in a Si/SiGe heterostructure with engineered meV-scale valley splitting and $^{28}$Si/$^{29}$Ge isotopic enhancement.
summary.result: Measured intrinsic charge noise improved by ~10× over prior work; multiqubit demonstrations show distance-5 code logical error rate $\approx 5 \times 10^{-3}$ with scaling factor $\Lambda_{5/3} = 4.7$ and [[4,2,2]] code throughput-fidelity comparable across all four basis preparations, with detector error model analysis confirming well-behaved, mostly low-weight errors.

papers.title: Efficient $n$-qubit entangling operations via a superconducting quantum router
papers.abstract: Quantum algorithms on near-term quantum processors are typically executed using shallow quantum circuits composed of one- and two-qubit gates. However, as circuit depth and gate number increase, gate imperfections and qubit decoherence begin to dominate, limiting algorithmic complexity. An alternative approach is to explore gates involving more than two qubits. In previous work (X. Wu et al., Physical Review X 14, 041030 (2024)), we demonstrated a new superconducting qubit architecture with user-selectable two-qubit interactions via a reconfigurable router, used to connect pairs of qubits. Here, we leverage this novel architecture to realize programmable and efficient multi-qubit operations involving more than two qubits, resulting in faster preparation of multi-qubit entangled states with good fidelities. We also successfully apply model-free reinforcement learning to perform multi-qubit gates, including training a two-qubit controlled-Z gate as well as three-qubit controlled-SWAP and controlled-controlled-phase (Fredkin and Toffoli) gates. Higher $n$th-order gates may also be feasible, using our high-connectivity router design. This could provide a more efficient and higher-fidelity implementation of complex quantum algorithms and a more practical approach to quantum computation.

similar_to.title: Universal Hamiltonian control in a planar trimon circuit

summary.summary: This work demonstrates efficient multi-qubit entangling operations on a superconducting quantum processor with a central reconfigurable router, achieving three- and four-qubit W states with fidelities $ac{97.72(3)\\\\ \text{%}$ and $94.70(4)\\\\ \text{%}$ in single-step interactions, and using model-free reinforcement learning (PPO) to synthesize native three-qubit gates. The RL-trained controlled-Z gate reaches $96.56 \text{ %} \pm 0.12 \text{ %}$ fidelity (25 % infidelity reduction versus hand-tuned), while the controlled-SWAP and controlled-controlled-phase gates achieve $85.74(78) \text{ %}$ and $84.59(75) \text{ %}$ respectively, outperforming decomposition into two-qubit gates.
summary.motivation: Multi-qubit native gates offer higher parallelism and reduced gate counts compared to decompositions into Clifford gates, enabling faster quantum error correction cycles and more complex algorithms on near-term processors where gate depth and decoherence dominate performance.
summary.method: Using simultaneous dynamic tuning of four reconfigurable switches in a central router to mediate many-to-many couplings, the authors prepare multi-qubit states via single-excitation evolution, synthesize entangling gates through flux-pulse optimization with the PPO reinforcement learning algorithm integrated with cross-entropy benchmarking (OXEBIT method), and encode control in piecewise-constant pulse segments with 8 samples per pulse.
summary.result: Three-qubit W and GHZ states prepared in $9.3$ and $19.6$ ns achieve higher fidelity than prior sequential methods (97.72 % vs. 93.87 % for three qubits); RL-optimized CZ gate surpasses hand-tuned performance with 96.56 % fidelity; three-qubit CSWAP (85.74 %) outperforms estimated decomposition fidelity below 75 %; decoherence limits gate errors at 8–10 % out of total 14–15 % infidelity, with training requiring $\sim 2000$ epochs ($\sim 19$ hours wall time for CZ).

papers.title: Towards Ultra-High-Rate Quantum Error Correction with Reconfigurable Atom Arrays
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction is widely believed to be essential for large-scale quantum computation, but the required qubit overhead remains a central challenge. Quantum low-density parity-check codes can substantially reduce this overhead through high-rate encodings, yet finite-size instances with practical logical error rates often achieve encoding rates only around or below $1/10$. Here, building on a recent ultra-high-rate construction by Kasai, we identify new structural conditions on the underlying affine permutation matrices that make encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ compatible with efficient implementation on reconfigurable neutral atom arrays. These conditions define a co-designed family of ultra-high-rate quantum codes that supports efficient syndrome extraction and atom rearrangement under realistic parallel control constraints. Using a hierarchical decoder with high accuracy and good throughput, we study the performance under a circuit-level noise model with $p=0.1\%$, achieving per-logical-per-round error rates of $1.3_{-0.9}^{+3.0} \times 10^{-13}$ with a $[[2304,1156,\leq 14]]$ code and $2.9_{-1.5}^{+3.1} \times 10^{-11}$ with a $[[1152,580,\leq 12]]$ code. We compare these codes against a heuristic Pareto frontier for finite-blocklength codes relating block length, encoding rate, and logical error rates, and find that our codes lie near the frontier. These results approach the teraquop regime, highlighting the promise of this code family for practical ultra-high-rate quantum error correction.

similar_to.title: Quantum error correction at ultra-low overhead

summary.summary: This work co-designs ultra-high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes with reconfigurable neutral-atom hardware, achieving encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ at block lengths $\sim 1000$ qubits by constraining affine permutation matrices to commute with reference maps whose orbits decompose into simple atom rearrangements. Circuit-level simulations at $p = 0.1\%$ yield per-logical-per-round error rates of $1.3_{-0.9}^{+3.0} \times 10^{-13}$ for the $[[2304,1156,\leq 14]]$ code and $2.9_{-1.5}^{+3.1} \times 10^{-11}$ for the $[[1152,580,\leq 12]]$ code using a hierarchical decoder combining belief propagation with integer-programming fallback.
summary.motivation: Quantum error correction requires reducing qubit overhead; quantum LDPC codes promise high rates exceeding $1/10$, but prior constructions achieved only $\sim 1/10$ at practical block lengths, and it was unclear whether Kasai's recent ultra-high-rate affine-permutation construction (rate $\sim 1/2$, distance $>30$ at $n \sim 9000$) could yield competitive performance on near-term platforms with realistic hardware constraints.
summary.method: Starting from Kasai's block-circulant CSS construction over affine permutations $x \mapsto ax + b \pmod{P}$, we identify codes where all transition permutations commute with a reference APM, decomposing into orbit-wise cyclic shifts plus small inter-orbit permutations compilable into $2$–$3$ crossed-AOD moves rather than $O(\log P)$ moves. Finite-size search enforces girth $\geq 6$, structured transitions, and verified distance bounds, yielding instances with rates $\approx 0.50$ at $n \in \{1152, 2304, 4608\}$.
summary.result: The $[[2304,1156,\leq 14]]$ code achieves logical error rate $1.3_{-0.9}^{+3.0} \times 10^{-13}$ per logical qubit per round at circuit-level noise $p = 0.1\%$ with 392 million shots (1 error observed), approaching the teraquop regime; codes lie near the Pareto frontier predicted by heuristic finite-blocklength estimates, with syndrome extraction completing in $\sim 8$–$10$ ms using realistic atom transport.
